column2: What does the standardized test statistic measure in a significance test for a proportion?
column3: How far the sample proportion falls from the population mean in raw units
column4: How many standard deviations the sample proportion is from the null value
column5: The likelihood that the null hypothesis is actually true given the data
column6: The probability of observing the exact sample proportion in future samples

column2: Why do we use the null hypothesis value rather than the sample proportion in the denominator of the test statistic?
column3: The formula sheet only lists one version so there is no choice involved
column4: Using the sample value would always produce a test statistic equal to zero
column5: The sample proportion is too unreliable to use in any statistical formula
column6: We assume the null hypothesis is true until the evidence convinces us otherwise

column2: Which of the following best describes the p-value of a significance test?
column3: The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the observed sample data
column4: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is false for the given population
column5: The probability of the observed result or more extreme by chance alone assuming H0 is true
column6: The probability that the sample was not randomly selected from the population

column2: A student says a p-value of 0.04 means there is a 4% chance the null hypothesis is true. What is wrong with this claim?
column3: The p-value actually measures the chance the alternative hypothesis is true instead
column4: The p-value should be doubled before interpreting it for any significance test
column5: The p-value measures the probability that the sample was biased during collection
column6: The p-value assumes H0 is true and measures how surprising the data would be

column2: When the alternative hypothesis uses a greater-than direction, how is the p-value found?
column3: By finding the area to the right of the test statistic on the standard normal curve
column4: By finding the area to the left of the test statistic on the standard normal curve
column5: By finding the area in both tails beyond the test statistic on the normal curve
column6: By finding the area between the test statistic and zero on the standard normal curve

column2: When the alternative hypothesis uses a less-than direction, how is the p-value found?
column3: By finding the area to the right of the test statistic on the standard normal curve
column4: By finding the area to the left of the test statistic on the standard normal curve
column5: By finding the area in both tails beyond the test statistic on the normal curve
column6: By finding the total area under the curve and subtracting the test statistic value

column2: When the alternative hypothesis uses a not-equal-to direction, how is the p-value found?
column3: By finding the area in one tail and reporting that single tail area as the p-value
column4: By finding the area between the negative and positive test statistic on the curve
column5: By finding the area to the right of the test statistic regardless of its sign
column6: By finding the area in one tail and then doubling it to account for both directions

column2: Why does a two-sided test require finding area in both tails of the normal distribution?
column3: Because the standard normal curve is symmetric so both tails must always be used
column4: Because evidence in either direction away from the null supports a not-equal-to alternative
column5: Because two-sided tests always produce larger test statistics than one-sided tests do
column6: Because the null hypothesis in a two-sided test specifies two different parameter values

column2: A one-sided test produces a p-value of 0.03 for a given data set. If the same data were used in a two-sided test, the p-value would be:
column3: 0.015 because a two-sided test splits the tail area into two equal halves
column4: 0.03 because the direction of the test does not change the resulting p-value
column5: 0.09 because a two-sided test triples the area to account for additional uncertainty
column6: 0.06 because a two-sided test doubles the one-tail area to include both directions

column2: What does the numerator of the test statistic formula (p-hat minus p0) represent?
column3: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution under the null hypothesis
column4: The probability of observing the sample proportion in a random sample from H0
column5: The number of successes in the sample divided by the total sample size observed
column6: The raw distance between the observed sample result and the null hypothesis value

column2: What does the denominator of the test statistic formula represent?
column3: The difference between the sample proportion and the hypothesized population value
column4: The typical amount that sample proportions vary from p0 when H0 is true
column5: The probability that a randomly selected sample would match the null hypothesis
column6: The margin of error used to construct a confidence interval for the proportion

column2: A researcher obtains a test statistic of z = 0. What does this tell us about the sample?
column3: The sample proportion is exactly equal to the value stated in the null hypothesis
column4: The null hypothesis has been proven true and no further analysis is required
column5: The conditions for performing the significance test have not been properly met
column6: The alternative hypothesis is definitely false and should be immediately rejected

column2: If the test statistic moves farther from zero, what happens to the p-value?
column3: The p-value gets smaller because the observed result is more unusual under the null hypothesis
column4: The p-value stays the same because it depends only on the direction of the alternative
column5: The p-value increases because extreme results are more common under the null hypothesis
column6: The p-value doubles because both tails must be considered regardless of the alternative

column2: A smaller p-value indicates which of the following about the evidence in the sample?
column3: Weaker evidence against H0 because small probabilities suggest the data match H0 well
column4: Evidence that the sample size was too small to draw any meaningful conclusions
column5: No change in evidence because p-values do not measure the strength of evidence at all
column6: Stronger evidence against H0 because the data would be very surprising if H0 were true

column2: Which statement correctly describes how to interpret a p-value?
column3: State the probability of H0 being true and describe what the sample proportion was
column4: Assume H0 is true and state the probability of getting a result this extreme by chance
column5: State the probability that Ha is true given the sample proportion that was observed
column6: Assume Ha is true and state the probability that the sample was randomly selected

column2: When writing a p-value interpretation, why must you include the phrase 'by chance alone'?
column3: It clarifies that the result could occur due to random sampling variability under H0
column4: It indicates that the researcher did not use any technology to find the p-value
column5: It means the sample was selected using a convenience method rather than random sampling
column6: It shows that no conditions needed to be checked before performing the significance test

column2: When interpreting a p-value, a student writes 'the probability of getting exactly 60% choosing green.' What is missing?
column3: The student should say the probability of getting the test statistic not the proportion
column4: The student should replace the percentage with the corresponding z-score instead
column5: The student should state the probability of getting less than 60% not 60% itself
column6: The student should include 'or greater' or 'or more extreme' not just the exact value

column2: Which piece of information must always be included at the start of a p-value interpretation?
column3: A statement that the conditions for the significance test have been properly verified
column4: A statement of the sample proportion and the sample size used in the study design
column5: A statement assuming the null hypothesis is true as the basis for the probability
column6: A statement assuming the alternative hypothesis is true as the basis for the probability

column2: You can think of the p-value as a type of conditional probability. What is the condition?
column3: The condition is that the sample was randomly selected from the population of interest
column4: The condition is that the alternative hypothesis is the correct claim about the parameter
column5: The condition is that the null hypothesis is true for the population being studied
column6: The condition is that the significance level has been set at 0.05 before testing

column2: A researcher is testing whether a coin is unfair (Ha: p is not equal to 0.50). The sample gives p-hat = 0.35. Which values count as 'as extreme or more extreme'?
column3: Only sample proportions of 0.35 or less because the observed result was below 0.50
column4: Only sample proportions of 0.65 or greater because we mirror the result above 0.50
column5: Sample proportions of 0.35 or less and also 0.65 or greater in both directions
column6: Sample proportions between 0.35 and 0.65 because those are closer to the null value

column2: A significance test for a population proportion uses the standard normal (z) distribution to find the p-value. This is appropriate because:
column3: The sampling distribution of p-hat is approximately normal when the conditions are met
column4: The population from which the sample is drawn must follow a normal distribution exactly
column5: The standard normal distribution is the only distribution available on the formula sheet
column6: All hypothesis tests must use the standard normal distribution regardless of the statistic

column2: On the AP formula sheet, why are both a standard deviation and a standard error listed for p-hat?
column3: The standard deviation uses the true value of p while the standard error uses p-hat instead
column4: The standard deviation is for large samples and the standard error is for small samples
column5: The standard deviation is for one-sided tests and the standard error is for two-sided tests
column6: The standard deviation and standard error formulas always produce the exact same values

column2: For a significance test about a proportion, which formula do we use from the formula sheet?
column3: The standard error formula with p-hat because it comes directly from the observed data
column4: The standard deviation formula with the null value substituted for p as the true value
column5: Either formula because the choice does not affect the resulting test statistic at all
column6: A completely different formula that is not listed on the formula sheet for proportions

column2: A student uses p-hat instead of p0 in the denominator of the test statistic. What error have they made?
column3: They calculated a confidence interval margin of error instead of the correct test statistic
column4: They used the wrong distribution to find the p-value from the resulting test statistic
column5: They used the standard error formula when they should have used the standard deviation formula
column6: They accidentally set up a two-sided test when the alternative hypothesis was one-sided

column2: Which of the following is needed to compute the test statistic for a one-sample z-test for a proportion?
column3: The sample proportion, the null hypothesis value, and the total number of observations
column4: The population proportion, the alternative hypothesis value, and the significance level
column5: The confidence level, the sample proportion, and the margin of error for the estimate
column6: The sample mean, the population standard deviation, and the total number of observations

column2: A test statistic of z = 2.8 would produce which type of p-value for a one-sided greater-than test?
column3: A large p-value indicating the data are consistent with what H0 predicts
column4: A p-value of exactly 0.05 because 2.8 is the critical value at that level
column5: A small p-value indicating the data would be unusual if H0 were actually true
column6: A negative p-value indicating the data fall in the opposite direction from Ha

column2: Suppose two studies test the same null hypothesis and one produces z = 1.2 while the other produces z = 2.9. Which study has stronger evidence against H0?
column3: The study with z = 1.2 because a smaller test statistic means a more significant result
column4: The study with z = 2.9 because a larger test statistic produces a smaller p-value
column5: Both studies provide equally strong evidence because they test the same null hypothesis
column6: Neither study provides evidence against H0 because both z-scores are positive values

column2: A p-value interpretation for a two-sided test must differ from a one-sided interpretation by including:
column3: A reference to evidence in either direction away from the null hypothesis value
column4: A reference to only the direction in which the sample proportion actually fell
column5: A statement that the significance level was doubled before comparing to the p-value
column6: A statement that the test statistic was divided by two before finding the area

column2: The general form of a standardized test statistic given on the AP formula sheet is:
column3: Sample size minus degrees of freedom divided by the total number of parameters tested
column4: Statistic minus parameter divided by the standard error of the statistic in question
column5: Parameter minus statistic divided by the standard deviation of the population data
column6: Statistic plus parameter divided by the margin of error for the confidence interval

column2: A researcher finds a p-value of 0.52. Which interpretation of this result is most accurate?
column3: The observed result would be fairly common under H0 so the data provide weak evidence against it
column4: The null hypothesis is definitely true because the p-value is greater than 0.50
column5: The alternative hypothesis has a 52% chance of being correct based on the sample data collected
column6: The test is invalid because p-values greater than 0.50 indicate a violation of conditions

column2: A student claims that a p-value tells you whether your sample was randomly selected. Is this correct?
column3: Yes because the p-value measures how well the random sampling procedure actually worked
column4: Yes because a small p-value means the sample was not truly random from the population
column5: No because the p-value measures how surprising the data are under H0 not sampling quality
column6: No because the p-value measures the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true

column2: When we say the p-value measures results 'as extreme or more extreme,' what does 'extreme' mean?
column3: Results that are closer to the null hypothesis value than the observed sample proportion
column4: Results that are farther from the null value in the direction specified by the alternative
column5: Results that have larger sample sizes than the sample that was actually collected
column6: Results that violate the conditions required for performing the significance test

column2: Which of the following would produce the smallest p-value in a one-sided test with Ha: p > 0.5?
column3: A sample proportion slightly above 0.5 with a small sample size from the population
column4: A sample proportion equal to exactly 0.5 with a very large sample from the population
column5: A sample proportion well above 0.5 with a large sample size from the population
column6: A sample proportion well below 0.5 with a large sample size from the population

column2: Why is it important to state the direction of the alternative hypothesis before collecting data?
column3: Because the direction determines whether you find area in one tail or in both tails
column4: Because changing the direction after seeing data does not affect the p-value at all
column5: Because the null hypothesis value changes depending on the direction you choose for Ha
column6: Because the formula for the test statistic is different for each direction of Ha

column2: A p-value does NOT tell us which of the following?
column3: The probability of observing data this extreme or more extreme under the null hypothesis
column4: Whether the observed result would be surprising if the null hypothesis were actually true
column5: The direction in which the sample result deviated from the null hypothesis parameter value
column6: The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data from the sample collected
